module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Pollock's (tetrahedral numbers) conjecture

Every positive integer is the sum of at most 5 tetrahedral numbers.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pollock%27s_conjectures)
- [A797](https://oeis.org/A797)
- L. E. Dickson, *History of the Theory of Numbers, Vol. II: Diophantine Analysis*, Dover (2005), pp. 22–23
- Frederick Pollock, *On the extension of the principle of Fermat's theorem on the polygonal numbers to the higher order of series whose ultimate differences are constant*, Abstracts of the Papers Communicated to the Royal Society of London **5** (1850), 922–924
- H. E. Salzer and N. Levine, *Table of integers not exceeding 100000 that are not expressible as the sum of four tetrahedral numbers*, Math. Comp. **12** (1958), 141–144
- [MathWorld: Pollock's Conjecture](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/PollocksConjecture.html)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace PollocksConjecture

open scoped BigOperators

/-  ## Definitions -/

/-- The $n$-th tetrahedral number: $T_n = \frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{6}$. -/
def tetrahedral (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  n * (n + 1) * (n + 2) / 6

/-  ## Auxiliary definition -/

/-- The set of natural numbers that are **not** a sum of $4$ tetrahedral numbers. -/
def NotSumOfFourTetrahedral : Set ℕ :=
  {N : ℕ | ∀ f : Fin 4 → ℕ, N ≠ ∑ i, tetrahedral (f i)}

/-  ## Statements -/

/--
Pollock's (tetrahedral numbers) conjecture:
every integer is the sum of at most $5$ tetrahedral numbers.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem pollock_tetrahedral (N : ℕ) :
    ∃ f : Fin 5 → ℕ, N = ∑ i, tetrahedral (f i) := by
  sorry

/--
Salzer–Levine strengthening (as stated on Wikipedia/OEIS):
there are exactly $241$ integers that are not a sum of $4$ tetrahedral numbers, and the largest is $343867$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem pollock_tetrahedral.salzer_levine :
    IsGreatest NotSumOfFourTetrahedral 343867 := by
  sorry

/-- As stated on Wikipedia/OEIS (A797), the set of exceptions has cardinality $241$. -/
@[category textbook, AMS 11]
theorem pollock_tetrahedral.ncard_exceptions :
    type_of% pollock_tetrahedral.salzer_levine ↔
    NotSumOfFourTetrahedral.ncard = 241 := by
  sorry

end PollocksConjecture

findings.description: The Salzer–Levine reference in the module docstring (line 30) misquotes the paper's title as “Table of integers not exceeding 100000 ...”. The actual bound in the title is 1000000. This is a bibliographic error; the mathematical declarations are unaffected.
findings.source_evidence: MathWorld's references and Crossref's record for DOI 10.1090/S0025-5718-1958-0099756-3 give the title “Table of integers not exceeding 1000000 that are not expressible as the sum of four tetrahedral numbers”, Mathematics of Computation 12 (1958), 141–144. https://mathworld.wolfram.com/PollocksConjecture.html ; https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0025-5718-1958-0099756-3
findings.suggested_fix: Change 100000 to 1000000 in the Salzer–Levine reference.

reformulations.difference: The source quantifies over positive integers and allows at most five tetrahedral summands. Lean quantifies over all natural numbers and uses exactly five indexed summands with unrestricted natural indices.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: tetrahedral 0 = 0, so a representation with at most five positive tetrahedral numbers can be padded with zeros, and zero-indexed terms can conversely be deleted. The additional N = 0 case is represented by five zeros. A full equivalence with the positive-integer, at-most-five-positive-summands formulation was proved independently in /workspace/review/proofs.lean.

reformulations.difference: The source's exceptions are numbers not representable by at most four tetrahedral numbers; the definition excludes representations indexed by Fin 4.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Zero-padding and deleting zero terms identify these representation predicates exactly. The equivalence with nonexistence of a list of at most four positive tetrahedral summands was proved in Lean. In particular, zero is not an extra exception.

reformulations.difference: The theorem states only that 343867 is the greatest exception, without explicitly conjoining the cardinality 241 mentioned in its docstring and the sources.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The exceptions through 343867 are a known finite set of exactly 241 elements, including 343867. An independent exhaustive computation through 1000000 reproduced the OEIS b-file exactly. Thus the greatest-element assertion forces the whole exception set to equal this prefix and have cardinality 241. Conversely, ncard = 241 forces finiteness, and containing this 241-element prefix leaves no room for further exceptions, so 343867 is greatest. This also validates ncard_exceptions as an auxiliary equivalence. The general set-theoretic equivalence was proved in Lean under the finite-prefix facts, but the concrete enumeration was not certified in Lean.

sources_consulted: L. E. Dickson, History of the Theory of Numbers, Vol. II, pp. 22–23, and the tetrahedral-number definition on p. 4; https://archive.org/download/historyoftheoryo02dickuoft/historyoftheoryo02dickuoft_djvu.txt
Crossref bibliographic metadata for Pollock, DOI 10.1098/rspl.1843.0223, retrieved by title query.

Local Mathlib sources: Mathlib/Data/Set/Card.lean (Set.ncard and its finiteness lemmas), Mathlib/Order/Bounds/Defs.lean (IsGreatest and upperBounds); Lean/Elab/BuiltinTerm.lean (type_of% elaboration).
review.notes: All five declarations were checked. No mathematical misformalization or stale status was found. Lean checks verified exact divisibility of n(n+1)(n+2) by 6, zero cases, the first four-summand exception 17, and a five-summand representation of 17. The textbook tag on ncard_exceptions concerns the valid equivalence, not an unconditional solution of the cardinality conjecture. The full OEIS entry and AMS Salzer–Levine paper were blocked by Cloudflare; the other cited sources, accessible OEIS data, Crossref metadata, and independent computation sufficed to settle the declarations' faithfulness.
